about: Fill in every "answer"; the tool refuses until each one is filled. The "recommended" values are suggestions and are never read by the tool.

cutoffs.question: From which percentile of its own history does a reading take ratings 2, 3, 4 and 5? Four numbers, each above the last, between 0 and 100.
cutoffs.why: A reading above the median is at least a 2, and the top two ratings sit in the tail: the Fed's Financial Stability Report speaks of the upper quartile and the 90th percentile, and the Fed staff heat map (Aikman et al. 2015) drew lines at the 65th and 85th, with a red zone at the 80th.

on_the_line.question: A reading exactly on a cut-off: does it take the worse rating or the better one? "worse" or "better".
on_the_line.why: The tool exists to warn; a tie goes to the warning. The loss thresholds ask the same question.

history.question: Which history is each reading measured against? "full" for everything the publisher has, or {"years": N} for the last N years up to the latest reading.
history.why: Every series starts in a different year, so a fixed window would cut the long ones short; the start of each history is shown beside every rating, as the regulators do.

change_months.question: Over how many months is a change counted? A whole number. Weekly and daily series count whole weeks (12 months is 52), as FRED does: a day with no reading that many weeks before has no change.
change_months.why: A year: it takes out the seasons, and the report reads homeowner's insurance and revolving credit over a year.

show_sahm.question: Show the Sahm reading beside the national unemployment rate? true or false. It is shown, not rated.
show_sahm.why: It is the best-known published trigger for unemployment (0.50 points, Sahm 2019), and the report records its false alarm of 2024, so a reader should see it beside the rating rather than instead of it.

change_for.question: Which series rated on their place in history also get a rating for their change? "all", or a list of series keys. Series rated on their change only always get it.
change_for.why: The report's first rule: unemployment is lowest just before recessions, so its level alone reads 1 Low at the turn; the change carries the signal, and the same holds for spreads and claims.

directions.question: For each reading the research leaves open: which way is stress? "higher is worse", "lower is worse" or "not rated".
directions.why: Prices: rising is worse for borrowers. House prices: stretched when high against income, stressed when falling (the report's second rule). Mortgage rate: higher is worse for payments. Revolving credit: faster growth is the build-up. Business loan demand: weaker is worse, the least certain of these.
